title: Predicting good probabilities with supervised learning
venue: Proceedings of the 22nd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML '05), Bonn, Germany, 7-11 August 2005. New York: ACM Press
harvard_reference: Niculescu-Mizil, A. and Caruana, R. (2005) 'Predicting good probabilities with supervised learning', Proceedings of the 22nd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML '05). Bonn, Germany, 7-11 August 2005. New York: ACM Press, pp. 625-632. doi:10.1145/1102351.1102430.
abstract_summary: The authors compare the probability estimates produced by ten supervised learning algorithms (SVMs, neural nets, decision trees, k-NN, bagged trees, random forests, boosted trees, boosted stumps, naive Bayes, logistic regression) against true posterior probabilities on eight binary classification problems, using reliability diagrams and prediction histograms. Maximum-margin methods (boosted trees, boosted stumps, SVMs) push predicted probabilities away from 0 and 1, producing a characteristic sigmoid-shaped distortion; naive Bayes has the opposite distortion; neural nets, bagged trees and logistic regression are well calibrated without post-processing. Two calibration methods are evaluated, Platt scaling (sigmoid fit) and isotonic regression (monotone piecewise-constant fit via PAV), including a learning-curve analysis of how much calibration data each needs. Platt scaling wins with small calibration sets (below roughly 200-1000 cases) because isotonic regression overfits; with 1000+ cases isotonic regression is as good or better. After calibration, boosted trees, random forests and SVMs predict the best probabilities.

claims_supported.claim: Boosted trees and SVMs produce distorted (sigmoid-shaped) probability estimates that benefit from Platt scaling or isotonic regression, whereas logistic regression and bagged trees are naturally well calibrated; isotonic regression needs larger samples than Platt scaling.
claims_supported.where: All three parts are stated explicitly. (a) Sigmoid distortion of boosted trees and SVMs and benefit from calibration: Abstract ('maximum margin methods such as boosted trees and boosted stumps push probability mass away from 0 and 1 yielding a characteristic sigmoid shaped distortion'); Section 1 names SVMs, boosted trees and boosted stumps; Section 4 (pp. 3 and 6) says boosted stumps and SVMs 'exhibit distinctive sigmoid-shaped reliability plots' and 'Both Platt Scaling and Isotonic Regression are effective at fitting this sigmoidal shape'; Section 6 / Figure 8 reports boosted trees, SVMs, boosted stumps and naive Bayes are 'dramatically improved by calibration'. (b) Logistic regression and bagged trees well calibrated: Section 4 (pp. 4-5): logistic regression and bagged trees 'are well calibrated initially and post-calibration does not help them on most problems'; Section 5 lists 'neural nets, bagged trees, and logistic regression' as methods for which neither calibration method helps much; Section 6: 'Calibration does not help bagged trees'. (c) Isotonic regression needs more data: Section 5 (learning-curve analysis, Figure 7): with calibration sets 'less than about 200-1000 cases, Platt Scaling outperforms Isotonic Regression with all nine learning methods' because isotonic regression 'is less constrained ... so it is easier for it to overfit'; with '1000 or more points' isotonic regression is 'as good as, or better than' Platt scaling. Section 7: 'Platt Scaling is most effective when the data is small, but Isotonic Regression is more powerful when there is sufficient data to prevent overfitting.' Note the abstract itself names only neural nets and bagged trees as well calibrated; logistic regression is confirmed in the body (Sections 4 and 5), so cite the paper generally rather than the abstract alone for that element.
